Testimony in Support of
Resolve, Directing the Department of Health and Human Services to Apply for a Waiver from the Federal Government for the Medicaid Limitation on
Payment to a Facility with More than 16 Inpatient Beds for Psychiatric Treatment - LD 563 March 24th, 2025
Good morning, Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and honorable members of the Committee on Health and Human Services. My name is Adam BloomPaicopolos. I am a resident of Wells and am proud to serve as the Executive Director of the Alliance for Addiction and Mental Health Services, Maine (the Alliance). The Alliance is the statewide association representing Maine's community-based behavioral health agencies who provide much-needed mental health and substance use services to over 80,000 children, adults, and families annually. The Alliance advocates for the implementation of sound policies and evidence-based practices that serve to enhance the quality and effectiveness of our behavioral health care system.
On behalf of the Alliance, I am here today to speak in support of LD 563, "Resolve, Directing the Department of Health and Human Services to Apply for a Waiver from the Federal Government for the Medicaid Limitation on Payment to a Facility with More than 16 Inpatient Beds for Psychiatric Treatment".
The institutions for mental diseases (IMD) Medicaid payment exclusion has been in place in Medicaid statute since 1965. An IMD is defined as a hospital, nursing facility, or other institution of more than 16 beds that is primarily engaged in providing diagnosis, treatment, or care of persons with mental diseases, which includes substance use disorders (SUDs). However, Maine sought and successfully received the waiver for IMD for SUD services in 2019. This waiver, combined with the recent rate reform, is allowing Maine to expand its capacity to serve those with substance use disorder in residential settings. Just this month, DHHS announced it would be reapplying for its 1115 SUD waiver.i
Maine initially had sought the waiver for IMD for mental health as well, but due to the very valid and important concerns expressed by many advocates with lived experience, Maine withdrew that request. Particularly following the dissolution of the AMHI Consent Decree, re-institutionalization fears exist. I want to make sure I state for the record, that myself, the Alliance, and our members share in those concerns and would never want to see a return to the system of our past. Importantly, however, that is not what is being asked for in this resolve.
We have all seen that what a shortage of inpatient beds across the state has resulted in: individuals getting stuck in hospital emergency departments or our criminal justice system for weeks, sometimes months, before an appropriate level of care

While community-based care remains the ideal option for many, some individuals do require intensive, time-limited inpatient care--and we must ensure that those beds are available when needed. Additionally, this waiver would enable Maine to access additional federal Medicaid matching dollars, easing some of the burden on the state's MaineCare budget and bringing much-needed funding to our behavioral health system of care. Such a waiver can serve as a complement to community-based care that could provide investment to the full continuum of mental health services. If this bill is successful, Maine would join a growing list of states, inclusive of our New England neighbors, pursuing an IMD waiver for mental health--15 states currently operate an approved mental health IMD waiver (including New Hampshire and Vermont) while 11 states have pending waiver with CMS (including Massachusetts).ii Maine's behavioral health system must be able to move forward with expanding its capacity, accessing more federal dollars for MaineCare, and investing in community-based services to better prevent unnecessary emergency department long stays and criminal justice interactions. LD 563 represents an opportunity to do just that. At the same time, we must also keep front of mind the very real concerns on any action towards re-institutionalization. Both are possible at the same time, with the 1115 waiver development and public input process providing meaningful opportunities to ensure that Maine goes about this in a mindful way that is responsive to valid community concerns. Thank you for the opportunity to provide testimony this morning. I would be happy to answer any questions from the Committee. Respectfully,

The IMD waiver bill would go a long way to adding more needed liaisons and ACT teams.
Behavioral Health Liaisons serve the critical role of bridging the gap between law enforcement, individuals experiencing mental health crises
or substance use issues, and the community. The role of behavioral
health liaisons is diverse and complex. A few key areas of focus to
highlight the ways they help would be as follows:
l. Crisis intervention: When co-responding with officers to calls for
service regarding mental health, behavioral health, or substance use, the liaisons can ensure that the individuals receive appropriate care instead of being placed in jail or
facing punitive actions. Some behavioral health liaisons
provide an alternative response, meaning they can respond to calls for service that do not rise to the level of needing an officer present- this allows officers to remain available for high-priority calls. The alternative response focuses on ensuring appropriate care is found for the individual.
2. De-escalation: Behavioral health liaisons are trained in de-
escalation techniques, which can help calm potentially volatile situations. This reduces the risk of injury or escalation of conflicts between officers and individuals experiencing
behavioral health issues.

3. Resource connection: Behavioral health liaisons have built relationships with key stakeholders in the community. They
can provide referrals to appropriate services; problem-solve barriers to engage in needed service and complete follow-ups
to ensure the connection was made. This helps reduce the
likelihood of repeat interaction with law enforcement as the
underlying issues are being addressed by individuals who are
trained specifically around mental health, behavioral health and substance use concerns.
4. Training for officers: A focus on increasing officers' awareness and
understanding of mental health and substance use disorders helps officers approach calls for service with increased empathy and knowledge. This aids in safety for officers, the
individual, and the community at large.
5. Improved outcomes: When a behavioral health liaison ensures an
individual receives the right care, it helps prevent unnecessary incarceration and improves overall public safety and health outcomes.
Ultimately, behavioral health liaisons help, reduce the strain on the criminal justice system and improve community outcomes.
Assertive Community Treatment (ACT) teams provide comprehensive,
community-based mental health care for individuals with severe mental
illness. ACT teams have been shown to directly benefit the community
in several key ways due to the range and intensity of the services they
provide
l. Reduced hospitalizations: ACT teams focus on helping individuals
manage their conditions in the community. By doing so often
there is a reduction in the frequency of hospital stays. The
reduction in hospital stays prevents overburdening psychiatric hospitals and emergency services. This also helps individuals

stay in their homes and communities. Community is key to
improving mental health
2. Improved quality of life: ACT teams provide personalized care to
support the individual with mental illness to improve or maintain their independence and wellbeing. Personalized care includes assisting with daily living skills, employment, housing, and social relationships all of which can lead to greater life satisfaction and stability.
3. Prevention of crises: By providing regular check-ins, therapy, and
monitoring, ACT teams reduce the need for emergency
interventions, which benefits individuals, first responders, and the community at large.
4. Reduced stigma: ACT team's help individuals live in their
communities rather than in institutions. The community can
see that individuals with severe mental health conditions can lead fulfilling lives with the right support.
5. Prevention of homelessness: By assisting individuals with mental
illness in maintaining stable housing and connecting them to
resources, ACT teams can help prevent homelessness, which is
a significant issue in many communities. They often provide
help with finding housing and addressing barriers to stability.
Overall, ACT teams benefit the community by improving the mental
health and well-being of individuals, reducing the burden on emergency and healthcare systems, and fostering at more supportive and inclusive environment for all residents.

Good Morning, my name is Chip Angell. I have been working to improve the treatment of the mentally ill since the early 2000's. I often came to these legislative hearings. At one in 2006 or so, I was asked by Richard Malaby to join an ad hoc group set off to hammer out a dispute over PTP before returning to the hearing where the committee could vote on our solution.
In that meeting we opened the application process to PTP from only the administrator of the hospital to Doctors, Judges, and several others. We also made several other modifications to the PTP law that improved access to treatment. While the legislature gave DHHS the responsibility of promoting it through education, notices and some rules and regulations. They haven't done anything. DHHS essentially ignores PTP.
While there are still 2 � PTP teams in Maine, we need at least 7. PTP is the robust out-patient treatment program that supports the seriously mentally ill in the least restrictive environment as required by law. It allows the seriously mentally ill to function without hospitalization, safely, in society, and under treatment where necessary.
The IMD Exclusion Waiver, the subject of LD563, and why we are here today, has within it the requirement that states who join will be required to establish and maintain robust out-patient programs. These are vital to an effective treatment effort.
Maine has the legislation and has the rules, but they aren't followed, few people know that this avenue of treatment exists. In fact with only the two teams, too many in Maine remain untreated.
Last month, I visited the Eagle Nest clubhouse in Ellsworth. Their director related to me that one of her employees had a mental health crisis herself and was in the emergency room waiting for a bed to open at a mental health hospital. After two weeks, unable to find her a bed, she was released to home...untreated and still unstable. It happens over and over again in Maine.
Our son died in 2010 at 38yrs old. He had paranoid Schizophrenia. He was a patient at Dorathy Dix, Spring Harbor, Acadia, and finally at Riverview. I had to have him arrested to get him a bed there. Chris also suffered from Anosogosnia. He didn't believe he was sick, so of course he would never go for treatment himself.
His college tennis coach believed Chris to be a world class tennis player. As a scholarship athlete at Indiana, he was the best tennis player in the Big Ten as a sophomore when his illness manifested itself. Chris finished college, he had ranked as high as 32 in the NCAA before graduating and then played briefly on the pro tour. But his untreated illness affected his life onward.
15 years later after some 14 hospitalizations in New Jersey, multiple arrests, a broken marriage and a wonderful daughter, we got him to move to Maine. By the way, New Jersey has now applied for this waiver for both substance abuse and mental health.
We bought and were running a restaurant in Brooklin Maine and believed that Maine was a better place for him. He joined us there and began teaching tennis in Ellsworth for a wonderfully patient owner of the club. He was always a good worker, our best dishwasher, a careful and eager prep cook, an entertaining and confident waiter, and once back in tennis he worked hard to become Maine's top ranked men's open player two years running.
But schizophrenia is relentless. It's uncureable, but treatable. Early treatment is key to reducing its effect. Every mental crisis, leads to further deteriorization. Treatment is finding the medication that works for that particular individual. It can take a month, even several months by trial and error.
Unfortunately, the IMD Exclusion prevents reimbursement to States for Mental patients in a hospital with more than 16 beds. Chris was never able to stay in a

hospital longer than a few days or maybe two weeks. Until, that is, Riverview, where a judge ordered a minimum of 30 days. The staff there spent his 30 days teaching him what to say to the judge to get released.
He was released without a discharge plan, with a prescription for meds he would never take at a pharmacy 100 miles from his home, and without them informing us. The Invega shot he was given at Riverview which he told us was the best, was not continued as it was falsely stated by the hospital administrator as not on the States approved list. Chris died some 40 days after discharge. He fell into a deep depression caused by a psychiatrist's miss prescribed medication.
I am one of hundred's maybe thousands of parents who can recite to you similar tragedies. And meanwhile there are another thousands of individuals living on the street, incarcerated, or at home untreated. They should not have the freedom to be sick as the Disability Rights group has convinced so many in the DHHS and the Governor to believe. A ludicrous concept that is the cause of so much distress, tragedy and deaths in Maine.
It doesn't happen so much in other places. New Jersey hasn't had a mental illness tragedy since 2004 when a police officer, untrained in CIT shot a mentally ill individual. New Jersey immediately established an arrest diversion program called Arrive Together. Now, all across the state, a trained mental health person is dispatched together with a CIT trained officer for all mental illness calls. Several police chiefs in Maine are trying to set up a similar program in their cities. I hope to talk to our Attorney General about this tomorrow at Chellie Pingree's town meeting where he will be a guest.
In Michigan, their Attorney General set up a similar Arrest Diversion program that dufuses crisis and where an arrest is necessary, much less frequently, jail is by passed and treatment is mandated. Their solutions depended on bypassing the DHHS and going through the AG office instead.
Back to the IMD Waiver....with something like 3-4 % of the world's population suffering from serious mental illness, a figure unchanged in human history, treatment is the first step. Taking the waiver with it's matching funds to support that robust out-patient program is unquestionably a logical first step. With mental patients time in treatment being paid by the federal government, the number of beds will increase. The homeless numbers, where it is estimated that 30% are mentally ill, will go down. The inmate population where some 40-50% are mentally ill and untreated will be cut almost in half. The revolving door to treatment will close.
Maine needs to regain its primary position it once held in treatment for the seriously mentally ill. We can't bring back those lost at Lewiston and the so many others whose lives have been destroyed. We can and have a responsibility to help those now with Serious Mental Illness and the others to come in the future.
Please support and forward LD563 to the legislature for passage.
Thank you.

Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services
Testimony in Support of LD 563 - "Resolve, Directing the Department of Health and Human Services to Apply for a Waiver from the Federal Government for the Medicaid Limitation on Payment to a Facility with More Than 16 Inpatient Beds for Psychiatric Treatment"
March 24, 2025
Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services. I am Deborah Laurie, City Manager of the City of Bangor, and I am providing testimony in support of LD 563, "Resolve, Directing the Department of Health and Human Services to Apply for a Waiver from the Federal Government for the Medicaid Limitation on Payment to a Facility with More Than 16 Inpatient Beds for Psychiatric Treatment."
The City of Bangor is home to two psychiatric hospitals, Northern Light Acadia Hospital and the Dorothea Dix Psychiatric Center. Both provide excellent care to Mainers experiencing psychiatric crisis. They, and all psychiatric facilities across Maine, face many challenges which could be effectively addressed by increased funding opportunities such as those created by the waiver of the Medicaid limitation on payments to facilities with more than 16 inpatient beds.
Bangor is also home to two hospitals, both of which routinely have emergency departments struggling under the burden of severely mentally ill patients with no appropriate placement. In far too many instances, without placement options, these individuals are discharged with no plan for housing or the intensive psychiatric services they so desperately need. They are essentially left to fend for themselves. Consequently, many join the growing ranks of homeless adults and youth on the streets of Bangor and most service center communities across the state.
Currently, federal law prohibits states from using Medicaid to pay for care provided in "institutions for mental disease" (IMDs), which are psychiatric hospitals or other residential treatment facilities that have more than 16 beds. This is the only part of federal Medicaid law that prohibits payment for the cost of providing medically necessary care because of the type of illness being treated or the number of beds in a facility. This exclusion has been in place since Medicaid's enactment in 1965, and it has resulted in unequal coverage of mental health care and likely contributes to the inability of psychiatric providers like those in our community to maintain or expand bed capacity in response to the ever-growing need.
We support any action the State can take to increase funding opportunities that could greatly expand bed capacity and improve treatment options for some of our most vulnerable citizens. With treatment capacity increased, our jails will no longer serve as the largest de facto psychiatric hospitals in the state.
On behalf of the Bangor City Council, I strongly urge you to pass LD 563 to improve the provision of psychiatric treatment across Maine. Thank you for your consideration.
Cara Pelletier, City Council Chair, cara.pelletier@bangormaine.gov Deborah Laurie, City Manager, debbie.laurie@bangormaine.gov

POSITION STATEMENT IN SUPPORT LD 563: Resolve, Directing the Department of Health and Human Services to Apply for a Waiver from
the Federal Government for the Medicaid Limitation on Payment to a Facility with More than 16
Inpatient Beds for Psychiatric Treatment

As the state's largest grassroots mental health advocacy organization, NAMI Maine supports the
passage of LD 563 regarding DHHS's application for the federal waiver of Medicaid limitations on payment to a facility with more than 16 inpatient beds for psychiatric treatment. As Maine continues to struggle to navigate the unmet mental health needs of its residents, limiting access to payment to facilities operating with more than 16 psychiatric beds is an unnecessary barrier to providing vital inpatient care for Maine residents. Since Medicaid's inception in 1965, there has been a restriction on psychiatric facilities, previously referred to as Institutions for Mental Diseases (IMDs), intended to prevent states from transferring the burden of mental health care costs to the federal government and attempting to encourage investment in community-based services. This restriction is known as the IMD Exclusion, which limits Medicaid funding to facilities with fewer than 16 psychiatric treatment beds.
With an approved waiver to the IMD Exclusion, Maine would be eligible to receive Medicaid reimbursement for treatment provided at larger facilities, currently inaccessible to many residents. Outside of the IMD Exclusion, Medicaid covers the cost of medically necessary care, highlighting the
disparity in access to care. This discriminatory exclusion has resulted in unequal coverage of mental
health treatments compared to other medical treatments. By seeking a waiver from the IMD Exclusion, we place the treatment decision~making in the hands of trained mental health professionals who have evaluated the necessity of an inpatient level of care. Without this waiver, we rely on a nearly 60-year-old policy that has left our local hospital emergency rooms overcrowded, often resulting in unnecessarily
long wait times and limited care for patients awaiting placement in an inpatient facility. We have the
opportunity to ease the burden on our systems of care by accessing a waiver that has been approved in other states, to which Maine is equally entitled.
While this application for an IMD Exclusion waiver will not solve the entirety of the struggles
within the mental health system, this is an important step forward to provide timely and appropriate
care to patients who have been assessed to need an inpatient level of care. This step enables our
overburdened emergency room staff to place patients more effectively earlier. We recognize and
emphasize that in many of these cases, prompt and evidence-based mental health treatments would decrease the number of individuals seeking inpatient-level care, and the waiver will assist with more
timely inpatient treatment. We must also ensure that there are services available for individuals to
engage in upon their discharge. The State of Maine has received and implemented an IMD waiver previously in 2019 and is
currently seeking to renew it for substance use disorders (SUD). This waiver has proven so successful in increasing access to care for individuals struggling with SUD that they are currently seeking to renew the
application. With the success demonstrated by the IMD waiver regarding SUD treatment and the outdated, stigmatizing policies the initial exclusions were based on, we urge the committee to support
LD 563.

SUMMARY

The Medicaid Institutions for Mental Disease (IMD) exclusion is an outdated, discriminatory federal rule that creates significant barriers to treatment for adults with severe mental illness. Under this rule, Medicaid payments to states are prohibited for non-geriatric adults receiving psychiatric care in a treatment facility with more than 16 beds.
Even with recent advances in mental health care afforded by the Affordable Care Act and federal parity legislation, the IMD exclusion remains the only section of federal Medicaid law that prohibits federal payment for medically necessary care simply because of the type of illness being treated. This categorically discriminatory rule is a leading cause of our national psychiatric hospital bed shortage and directly contributes to a host of negative consequences for those with the most severe mental illnesses.
BACKGROUND
The IMD exclusion was included in the law when Medicaid was enacted in 1965. At the time, there was hope that large inpatient facilities would be quickly rendered obsolete by advancements in new antipsychotic medications that allowed some people with serious mental illness to live safely in the community for the first time. The reasoning behind the IMD exclusion prohibiting reimbursement was thus twofold: disincentivize the treatment of the mentally ill in large institutions and shift the costs for psychiatric treatment from the federal government onto the states.
IMPACT
The economic impacts of the IMD exclusion have also been tremendous. While it does cost money to provide inpatient treatment to individuals with mental illness, cost savings from restricting inpatient care is largely an illusion.
